subject: english-literature
title: Modern Tragedy
welcome_lead: Can the common man be tragic? Miller, Williams and Brecht renew the form for the modern stage.
meta_desc: Modern tragedy — Miller, Williams and Brecht — at A-Level English Literature.
final_note: You have seen tragedy democratised — fall is no longer a privilege of kings.

concepts.def: Twentieth-century renewal of the tragic mode for ordinary protagonists (Miller, Williams, Ibsen).
Arthur Miller's 1949 essay arguing ordinary protagonists can be tragic; Willy Loman as exemplar.
Tragedy set within the family rather than the state (Death of a Salesman, A Streetcar Named Desire).
The gap between protagonist's beliefs and the audience's knowledge of doom.
Brecht's anti-cathartic theatre — alienation effect (Verfremdungseffekt) blocking emotional identification.
Postwar tragedies (Beckett, Camus) confronting meaninglessness without traditional resolution.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Miller's Tragedy and the Common Man (1949) defends the dignity of ordinary protagonists. Willy Loman's American Dream becomes his hamartia.

Modern tragedy democratises the form without abandoning its emotional structure.
Tennessee Williams's A Streetcar Named Desire (1947) sets Blanche DuBois's fall against post-war American class change. Domestic tragedy with mythic resonance.
Brecht rejected Aristotelian catharsis as politically anaesthetising. His epic theatre uses alienation devices (placards, songs, breaking the fourth wall) to keep audiences critical, not weeping.
